provenance: SYNTHETIC, hand-invented on 2026-10-23 for the open-source release. Every PR number, head SHA, reviewer login, path, diff hunk, review comment and note in this file was written from scratch about a fictional observatory's software (a Go telescope-time scheduler, a Rust image-calibration crate, a TypeScript booking portal, Python reduction scripts, SQL migrations and a CI workflow), reviewed by fictional reviewers whose logins start with 'fictional-'. It has no relation to any real repository, PR, person or review. It replaces an earlier synthetic set that had been paraphrased from a private review corpus, which made it unfit to publish. The shape is chosen to exercise the instrument: several cases per reviewer under the per-reviewer cap, APPROVED, COMMENTED and CHANGES_REQUESTED verdicts, MERGED and CLOSED PRs, all three expectation labels with expected-catch a minority, multi-line threads, single-line threads, and line-1 file-level comments with no hunk. Each finding's substance object is the output of classifySubstance in src/regression.ts on that comment, not a hand-typed value; the expectation labels and notes are the author's judgment, kept in regression-labels.json.

findings.text:
`sort.Slice` is not stable, and two proposals with the same grade and the same requested hours compare equal here, so their order depends on whatever order the database returned them in. That matters because the allocator is meant to be reproducible: the time allocation committee re-runs it from the same inputs to audit a night, and it would hand them a different schedule. Suggest a total order with the proposal id as the last key:
```go
if a.RequestedHours != b.RequestedHours {
	return a.RequestedHours < b.RequestedHours
}
return a.ID < b.ID
```
findings.note: Reproducibility follows from the comparator alone: anyone reading it can see there is no final tie-breaker.

findings.text: This stamps the block with the wall-clock date at the moment the allocator runs, not with the night it belongs to. findings.text: This module reads every calibrated frame of the night into one `numpy` array before combining. A long winter night on the wide-field camera is around 240 frames of 9576x6388 float32, which is roughly 58 GB, and the reduction nodes have 32 GB. It will be killed by the OOM reaper on exactly the nights we care most about. Suggest combining in row strips with `np.memmap` (or `astropy.io.fits` with `memmap=True`) so only one strip of every frame is resident at a time.
findings.plain: This module reads every calibrated frame of the night into one numpy array before combining. A long winter night on the wide-field camera is around 240 frames of 9576x6388 float32, which is roughly 58 GB, and the reduction nodes have 32 GB. It will be killed by the OOM reaper on exactly the nights we care most about. Suggest combining in row strips with np.memmap (or astropy.io.fits with memmap=True) so only one strip of every frame is resident at a time.
findings.note: A file-level comment with no hunk; the loading strategy and the frame size are both readable in the change.

findings.text: I would go with `sigma=2.5` here instead of 3.0. That said, the right number depends on how many frames the typical program takes, which this PR doesn't tell us.

findings.text: `semester.nights` are plain dates like `"2025-09-14"`, and `new Date()` parses a date-only string as midnight UTC. `toLocaleDateString` then renders it in the browser's zone, so anyone west of Greenwich (the southern partner site, for one) sees every night labelled as the day before and books the wrong one. Since these are calendar dates rather than instants, I would split the string into its parts, or pass `timeZone: "UTC"` in the options.
findings.plain: semester.nights are plain dates like "2025-09-14", and new Date() parses a date-only string as midnight UTC. toLocaleDateString then renders it in the browser's zone, so anyone west of Greenwich (the southern partner site, for one) sees every night labelled as the day before and books the wrong one. Since these are calendar dates rather than instants, I would split the string into its parts, or pass timeZone: "UTC" in the options.

findings.text: `scheduler/go.mod` still declares `go 1.21`, so the loop variable is shared across iterations and every goroutine takes `&tel` of the same variable. In practice they all end up polling the last telescope in the slice and the others are never checked, which means a dome fault at the first site would not mark it unavailable. Either bump the module to 1.22 or copy it inside the loop (`tel := tel`).

findings.text:
`exposure_ms / dark.exposure_ms` is integer division on `u32`, so a 90 s science frame matched to the 60 s dark gets a factor of 1, and a 45 s frame against the same dark gets 0, so nothing is subtracted at all. Thermal signal grows linearly with exposure time, which is the whole reason for scaling. Suggest doing it in floating point:
```rust
let factor = exposure_ms as f32 / dark.exposure_ms as f32;
```
findings.plain:
exposure_ms / dark.exposure_ms is integer division on u32, so a 90 s science frame matched to the 60 s dark gets a factor of 1, and a 45 s frame against the same dark gets 0, so nothing is subtracted at all. Thermal signal grows linearly with exposure time, which is the whole reason for scaling. Suggest doing it in floating point:
let factor = exposure_ms as f32 / dark.exposure_ms as f32;

findings.text: The cache key hashes `calib/Cargo.toml`, which only changes when someone edits a version range. A `cargo update` moves `Cargo.lock` but keeps the key, and because the cache action never overwrites an existing key, the saved `target/` stays frozen at the first run's dependencies and every later run recompiles whatever moved. Hash `calib/Cargo.lock` instead, or both files.

findings.text: This retries every 4xx, including the 409 the hold endpoint returns when another observer already holds the slot. Retrying a 409 cannot succeed, so the user waits through three backoffs (almost two seconds) before seeing the conflict, and a 400 from a malformed request is retried the same way. I would retry only on network errors, 429 and 5xx, and surface every other 4xx straight away.
findings.plain: This retries every 4xx, including the 409 the hold endpoint returns when another observer already holds the slot. Retrying a 409 cannot succeed, so the user waits through three backoffs (almost two seconds) before seeing the conflict, and a 400 from a malformed request is retried the same way. I would retry only on network errors, 429 and 5xx, and surface every other 4xx straight away.
findings.note: The 409 contract lives in the hold endpoint's handler in the same repository, so the evidence is reachable from the tree.
